# Important Terms and Ideas: Vagueness and Identity

**Vagueness**: The semantic property of predicates (and sometimes objects) whereby there are borderline cases for which it is neither determinately true nor determinately false that the predicate applies.

**Sorites paradox**: The puzzle generated by vague predicates: one grain does not make a heap; if n grains do not make a heap, neither do n+1; therefore no number of grains makes a heap — which is absurd.

**Epistemicism**: The view that vagueness is merely epistemic — there is always a precise fact of the matter (every predicate has precise extension), but we are ignorant of where the boundaries lie.

**Supervaluationism**: The view that a sentence is true (super-true) iff it is true on all permissible sharpenings of vague terms; false iff false on all sharpenings; otherwise indeterminate.

**Indeterminate identity**: The claim that it can be indeterminate whether a = b — that there is no fact settling whether two things are numerically identical. Evans's proof is designed to refute this.

**Metaphysical indeterminacy**: The view (Barnes, Williams) that indeterminacy is not merely semantic or epistemic but a genuine feature of reality — the world itself is metaphysically indeterminate in certain respects.

**Ontic vagueness (vague objects)**: The view that some objects are vaguely bounded — that it is not always determinate what is and is not a part of a given object. Clouds, rivers, and organisms are sometimes proposed as vague objects.

**Tolerance**: A property of vague predicates: a vague predicate P tolerates small differences in its subject — adjacent cases in a sorites series cannot differ in whether P applies. Tolerance, combined with transitivity, generates the sorites paradox.
